title: Genesis 29 — Ya'aqov at the well, the deception of Lavan, and the first sons of Le'ah

verdicts.reasoning: Literal 'lifted up his feet' matches ASV/Alter preservation of the editorially-marked nasa+raglav hapax variant; the smoothing to 'went on his journey' (KJV) is the deviation, not the WoH choice. Hebrew parses cleanly.
Routine narrative rendering; he'evahn gedolah / pi ha-be'er correctly preserved as 'great stone' / 'well's mouth'.
Verbal sequence rolled-watered-returned accurately rendered; perfect-consecutive forms preserved as iterative.
achai (my brothers) literally rendered; me-ayin (from where) standard.
Routine; ha-yda'tem rendered idiomatically as 'do you know'.
ha-shalom lo / shalom rendered 'is it well with him / it is well' — ASV-baseline.
hen od ha-yom gadol / lo et he'asef — 'lo, it is still high day; not the time the cattle should be gathered' — accurate.
lo nukhal ad asher ye'asfu — 'we cannot until... are gathered' — literal and accurate.
ro'ah hi rendered 'she was a shepherdess' — feminine participle of ra'ah (shepherd) correctly distinguished from ra'ah (see); a small but real philological win.
Triple repetition of 'Lavan his mother's brother' preserved (the Hebrew's editorially-marked emphasis); va-yigash / va-yagel sequence accurate.
va-yishaq va-yisa et-kolo va-yevk literal: 'kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept'; commentary correctly flags the inverted kiss-before-introduction type-scene editorial-move.
va-yaged ... va-tarotz va-tagged — 'told... and she ran and told' — accurate.
va-yarotz...va-ychabek...va-ynashek — 'ran...embraced...kissed' — fully literal.

atzmi u-vsari preserved literally as 'my bone and my flesh' (ASV); the NRSV/NJPS smoothing to 'flesh and blood' would dissolve the etzem-va-basar cross-corpus formula. Defensible and correctly chosen.
ha-khi achi atah / chinnam — 'because you are my kinsman / for nothing' — accurate.
ha-gedolah / ha-qetannah rendered 'elder / younger' — ASV-baseline, accurate.

rakkot rendered 'tender' (ASV/Alter) preserves the Hebrew's contested semantic range between weak (LXX astheneis, Rashi, NJPS) and lovely (Speiser, Onkelos). The choice is philologically-honest; commentary correctly surfaces all four readings. yefat to'ar v-yefat mar'eh accurately rendered as the doubled-construct beauty-formula.
va-ye'ehav / e'evadkha — 'loved / I will serve' — literal.
tov titti otah lakh mi-titti — comparative-construction 'better that I give... than that I give' — accurate.

k-yamim achadim b-ahavato otah rendered 'as a few days, for the love he had to her' — ASV-baseline preserving b-einav perception-formula and b-ahavato causal-clause. The Gen 11:1 / Gen 29:20 achadim verbal-echo is correctly identified in commentary.
havah et-ishti ki male'u yamai v-avo'ah eleha — 'give me my wife... that I may go in to her' — accurate; the va-avo'ah cohortative correctly rendered.
va-ye'esof... va-ya'as mishteh — 'gathered... made a feast' — literal.
va-yhi va-erev va-yiqach...va-yave...va-yavo — the terse three-verb sequence preserved without elaboration; matches the Hebrew's editorial-economy.
Zilpah-as-shifchah accurately rendered as 'maidservant'.

va-lamah rimitani rendered 'why have you deceived me' — verb ramah (deceive) correctly identified; commentary correctly flags the lexical-rhyme with Gen 27:35 b-mirmah (Ya'aqov's own deception of Yitzchaq). Editorially-essential observation.

ha-tze'irah / ha-bekhirah preserved literally as 'the younger / the firstborn' (against NJPS 'older'); the bekhir- root-link to Gen 27's bekhorah is essential for the editorial-irony and is correctly preserved. The chapter's narrative-structural pivot; commentary is exemplary.
male shvua zot rendered 'fulfill the week of this one' (ASV) — preserves the lexical-link to the broader shavua root; the bridal-week sense is conveyed by context and surfaced in commentary.
va-ya'as Ya'aqov ken va-ymalle shvua zot — 'did so and fulfilled her week' — literal; the seven-day-feast is correctly distinguished from the seven-year service-periods.
Bilhah-as-shifchah parallel to v 24.
va-ye'ehav gam et-Rachel mi-Le'ah rendered 'loved Rachel more than Le'ah' — the comparative-min construction correctly rendered.

va-yiftach et-rachmah rendered 'he opened her womb' — consensus formula. s'nu'ah rendered 'hated' (ASV-literal) is defensible; the comparative-construction reading (Deut 21:15; NRSV/NJPS 'unloved') is correctly flagged in commentary. The patach-rechem / atzar-rechem counter-pattern is correctly identified.
Re'uven aetiology: ki ra'ah YHWH b-onyi ('YHWH has looked upon my affliction') — wordplay on ra'ah + ben correctly surfaced in commentary; ASV-baseline phrasing accurate.
Shim'on aetiology: shama YHWH ki s'nu'ah anokhi ('YHWH has heard that I am hated') — wordplay shama + -on suffix correctly surfaced; the s'nu'ah re-deployment from v 31 correctly noted.

Levi aetiology: yilaveh ishi elai ('will my husband be joined to me') — wordplay on l-v-h root correctly identified; the woman-centered original vs cultic-deployment Num 18:2-4 correctly distinguished in commentary.

Yehudah aetiology: ha-pa'am odeh et-YHWH ('this time I will praise YHWH') — hiphil yadah → Yehudah correctly identified; the Y-H-W-D-H theophoric observation is sound (Y-H-W consonants visibly embedded); the verb-progression ra'ah→shama→lavah→yadah is verifiable. va-ta'amod mi-ledet closing-formula accurately rendered.

citations: Alter 1981 *The Art of Biblical Narrative* ch. 3
glossaryReview.reasoning: The three-instance type-scene (Gen 24 / Gen 29 / Exod 2) is critical-consensus since Alter 1981; the fixed components and per-instance variations are grammatically explicit at each locus. claim_type=direct is defensible — the convention is observable, not interpreted. AppliesTo correctly spans the three-corpus.

Cross-corpus distribution (Gen 2:23, Gen 29:14, Judg 9:2, 2 Sam 5:1, 19:13-14, 1 Chr 11:1) is verifiable by lexical search. The editorial-irony reading at Gen 29:14 — set-up for v 26 deception — is mainstream Alter/Sarna. claim_type=direct is appropriate; the formula's force is lexical, not interpreted.

All four readings (weak/tender/lovely/neutral-soft) are correctly attested and sourced; the WoH choice 'tender' (ASV/Alter) is the philologically-conservative middle position that preserves the Hebrew's semantic range. claim_type=direct is appropriate because the dispute itself, not a resolution, is the entry's content.

The achadim adjectival-plural at Gen 11:1 and Gen 29:20 is grammatically explicit and the verbal-echo is verifiable by lexical search. The b-einav perception-formula and b-ahavato causal-clause are unambiguous. The narrator-intervention reading is mainstream Alter/Sarna. claim_type=direct supported.

The cross-corpus chain (Gen 25:23 → 25:31-34 → 27:19 → 27:36 → 29:26 → 48:13-20) is verifiable verbatim in the Hebrew; the bekhir-/tza'ir lexical-pair is unambiguous. The reading is critical-consensus since Fokkelman 1975 and the foundational ironic-pivot of the Jacob-cycle. claim_type=direct is fully defensible — the irony rests on lexical observation, not on synthesis. LOAD-BEARING entry passes the highest-scholar bar.

The shavua=seven-day-period sense is lexically uncontested; the bridal-week deployment at Gen 29:27-28 is grammatically clear from context; Judg 14:12, 17 confirms the institution HB-internally; Greengus 1969 and de Vaux 1961 document the ANE Mesopotamian wedding-feast institution. claim_type=direct appropriate.

The patach+rechem construction is grammatically explicit; cross-corpus distribution (Gen 29:31, Gen 30:22, 1 Sam 1:5-6, 1:19-20) is verifiable. The paired open/close-the-womb pattern with the existing atzar-rechem entry is well-conceived. The s'nu'ah lexical-discussion correctly surfaces the Deut 21:15 comparative-construction case. claim_type=direct supported.

citations: BDB s.v. raah, shama, lavah, yadah
glossaryReview.reasoning: Each of the four folk-etymologies (Re'uven/Shim'on/Levi/Yehudah) is grammatically anchored in the verse's own *ki amrah* clause; the verb-progression ra'ah→shama→lavah→yadah and the subject-shift YHWH→husband→Le'ah are verifiable by inspection. The Yehudah Y-H-W-D-H theophoric observation is lexically explicit. Fokkelman 1975 is the foundational compositional-reading. claim_type=direct fully appropriate.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֥א יַעֲקֹ֖ב רַגְלָ֑יו וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ אַ֥רְצָה בְנֵי־קֶֽדֶם׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov lifted up his feet, and came to the land of the children of the east.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The chapter opens with two editorially-marked features.** *Va-yisa Ya'aqov raglav* — *and Ya'aqov lifted up his feet* — is a Genesis **hapax variant** on the patriarchal *nasa eynayim* (*lift the eyes*) seeing-formula tracked across the patriarchal arc (see [sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes](#sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes)). The standard formula governs *eynayim* (eyes) as its object; here the verb *nasa* (lift) governs *raglav* (his feet). The construction is unique to this verse in Genesis. ASV and KJV smooth to *went on his journey*; Alter (*Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 152) preserves *lifted up his feet* on the grounds that the variant is editorially-deliberate and rhymes with the chapter's later *va-yisa et-qolo va-yevk* (v 11, *and lifted up his voice and wept*) — an intra-chapter *nasa*-cluster. The WoH preserves the literal *lifted up his feet* against the ASV/KJV smoothing.

**Major: well-betrothal type-scene #3.** Verses 1-14 instantiate the Hebrew Bible's well-betrothal type-scene — the third of three canonical instances (Gen 24 Eliezer-Rivkah; Gen 29 Ya'aqov-Rachel, here, the most-elaborated; Exod 2:15-22 Mosheh-Tzipporah, the most-compressed). Alter (*The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 3) is the foundational reading; the convention's fixed components — bridegroom journeys to foreign land; arrives at a well; the woman arrives with a flock; water is drawn; she runs home; family welcomes the stranger — are all present here and individually-modified to characterize Ya'aqov. The full apparatus is at [well-betrothal-type-scene](#well-betrothal-type-scene). The chapter's opening verb-of-motion sets the scene's frame: Ya'aqov is now the **bridegroom-in-motion**, the convention's first slot.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֞רְא וְהִנֵּ֧ה בְאֵ֣ר בַּשָּׂדֶ֗ה וְהִנֵּה־שָׁ֞ם שְׁלֹשָׁ֤ה עֶדְרֵי־צֹאן֙ רֹבְצִ֣ים עָלֶ֔יהָ כִּ֚י מִן־הַבְּאֵ֣ר הַהִ֔וא יַשְׁק֖וּ הָעֲדָרִ֑ים וְהָאֶ֥בֶן גְּדֹלָ֖ה עַל־פִּ֥י הַבְּאֵֽר׃

i18n.en: And he looked, and behold, a well in the field, and lo, three flocks of sheep lying there beside it; for out of that well they watered the flocks; and the stone upon the well's mouth was great.

paragraphs.text: וְנֶאֶסְפוּ־שָׁ֣מָּה כָל־הָעֲדָרִ֗ים וְגָלֲל֤וּ אֶת־הָאֶ֙בֶן֙ מֵעַל֙ פִּ֣י הַבְּאֵ֔ר וְהִשְׁק֖וּ אֶת־הַצֹּ֑אן וְהֵשִׁ֧יבוּ אֶת־הָאֶ֛בֶן עַל־פִּ֥י הַבְּאֵ֖ר לִמְקֹמָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And there were all the flocks gathered; and they rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone back upon the well's mouth in its place.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ יַעֲקֹ֔ב אַחַ֖י מֵאַ֣יִן אַתֶּ֑ם וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ מֵחָרָ֖ן אֲנָֽחְנוּ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to them, My brothers, from where are you? And they said, We are from Charan.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם הַיְדַעְתֶּ֖ם אֶת־לָבָ֣ן בֶּן־נָח֑וֹר וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ יָדָֽעְנוּ׃

i18n.en: And he said to them, Do you know Lavan the son of Nachor? And they said, We know him.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לָהֶ֖ם הֲשָׁל֣וֹם ל֑וֹ וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ שָׁל֔וֹם וְהִנֵּה֙ רָחֵ֣ל בִּתּ֔וֹ בָּאָ֖ה עִם־הַצֹּֽאן׃

i18n.en: And he said to them, Is it well with him? And they said, It is well; and, behold, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הֵ֥ן עוֹד֙ הַיּ֣וֹם גָּד֔וֹל לֹא־עֵ֖ת הֵאָסֵ֣ף הַמִּקְנֶ֑ה הַשְׁק֥וּ הַצֹּ֖אן וּלְכ֥וּ רְעֽוּ׃

i18n.en: And he said, Lo, it is still high day, neither is it time that the cattle should be gathered together; water the sheep, and go and feed them.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְרוּ֮ לֹ֣א נוּכַל֒ עַ֣ד אֲשֶׁ֤ר יֵאָֽסְפוּ֙ כָּל־הָ֣עֲדָרִ֔ים וְגָֽלֲלוּ֙ אֶת־הָאֶ֔בֶן מֵעַ֖ל פִּ֣י הַבְּאֵ֑ר וְהִשְׁקִ֖ינוּ הַצֹּֽאן׃

i18n.en: And they said, We cannot, until all the flocks are gathered together, and they roll the stone from the well's mouth; then we water the sheep.

paragraphs.text: עוֹדֶ֖נּוּ מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֑ם וְרָחֵ֣ל ׀ בָּ֗אָה עִם־הַצֹּאן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאָבִ֔יהָ כִּ֥י רֹעָ֖ה הִֽוא׃

i18n.en: While he was yet speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep; for she was a shepherdess.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֡י כַּאֲשֶׁר֩ רָאָ֨ה יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶת־רָחֵ֗ל בַּת־לָבָן֙ אֲחִ֣י אִמּ֔וֹ וְאֶת־צֹ֥אן לָבָ֖ן אֲחִ֣י אִמּ֑וֹ וַיִּגַּ֣שׁ יַעֲקֹ֗ב וַיָּ֤גֶל אֶת־הָאֶ֙בֶן֙ מֵעַל֙ פִּ֣י הַבְּאֵ֔ר וַיַּ֕שְׁקְ אֶת־צֹ֥אן לָבָ֖ן אֲחִ֥י אִמּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Ya'aqov saw Rachel the daughter of Lavan his mother's brother, and the sheep of Lavan his mother's brother, that Ya'aqov went near, and rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the flock of Lavan his mother's brother.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשַּׁ֥ק יַעֲקֹ֖ב לְרָחֵ֑ל וַיִּשָּׂ֥א אֶת־קֹל֖וֹ וַיֵּֽבְךְּ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The kiss-before-introduction is the Gen 29 type-scene's most-distinctive editorial-move.** In Gen 24, Eliezer first asks for water, then gives jewelry, then asks Rivkah's lineage, then bows down in worship — the recognition-and-blessing sequence precedes any physical-contact (24:47). Here Ya'aqov **kisses Rachel first** — before he has identified himself to her, before she knows who he is, before any family-introduction. The inversion is editorially-deliberate: Ya'aqov, the love-struck protagonist of this type-scene's most-elaborated instance, breaks the convention's standard-sequence (Alter 1981 p. 58; 2004 p. 152).

**The *va-yisa et-qolo va-yevk* (lifted up his voice and wept) closure.** The verb *va-yisa* (lifted up) echoes v 1's *va-yisa Ya'aqov raglav* (lifted up his feet) — the chapter's intra-textual *nasa*-cluster. Crying at the moment of betrothal is editorially-unusual; readings divide: (i) relief at journey's-end (Speiser); (ii) overwhelm at the providential-meeting (Sarna); (iii) gendered-emotion that the narrative does not gloss (Alter — *the Bible characteristically declines to explain interior states*); (iv) the standard ANE kinship-recognition gesture (Westermann, citing parallels). The text's silence is editorially-marked: the kiss-and-weep is left to the reader.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּגֵּ֨ד יַעֲקֹ֜ב לְרָחֵ֗ל כִּ֣י אֲחִ֤י אָבִ֙יהָ֙ ה֔וּא וְכִ֥י בֶן־רִבְקָ֖ה ה֑וּא וַתָּ֖רָץ וַתַּגֵּ֥ד לְאָבִֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman, and that he was Rivkah's son; and she ran and told her father.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִי֩ כִשְׁמֹ֨עַ לָבָ֜ן אֶת־שֵׁ֣מַע ׀ יַעֲקֹ֣ב בֶּן־אֲחֹת֗וֹ וַיָּ֤רָץ לִקְרָאתוֹ֙ וַיְחַבֶּק־לוֹ֙ וַיְנַשֶּׁק־ל֔וֹ וַיְבִיאֵ֖הוּ אֶל־בֵּית֑וֹ וַיְסַפֵּ֣ר לְלָבָ֔ן אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Lavan heard the tidings of Ya'aqov his sister's son, that he ran to meet him, and embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. And he told Lavan all these things.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ לָבָ֔ן אַ֛ךְ עַצְמִ֥י וּבְשָׂרִ֖י אָ֑תָּה וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב עִמּ֖וֹ חֹ֥דֶשׁ יָמִֽים׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said to him, Surely you are my bone and my flesh. And he abode with him the space of a month.

paragraphs.commentary:
***Akh atzmi u-vsari atah* — *surely you are my bone and my flesh* — deploys the Hebrew Bible's standard fictive-kinship-confirmation formula.** The idiom is first deployed at Gen 2:23 (Adam's recognition of Chavvah: *etzem me-atzamai u-vasar mi-bsari*) and recurs at Judg 9:2 (Avimelekh to Shechem), 2 Sam 5:1 (the tribes to David), 2 Sam 19:13-14 (David to Yehudah and Amasa), and 1 Chr 11:1 (see [atzmi-u-vsari-kinship-formula](#atzmi-u-vsari-kinship-formula)).

**The deployment is editorially-ironic.** Lavan's kinship-claim in v 14 will be violated within the same chapter: by v 25 Lavan will have substituted Le'ah for Rachel under cover of the wedding-feast — the deception that the kinship-bond was supposed to preclude. The chapter's twin Lavan-statements (v 14 *atzmi u-vsari*; v 26 *lo ye'aseh khen bi-mqomenu*) form a deception-frame around the wedding-narrative: the kinship-claim establishes what the wedding-deception will violate. The *akh* (*surely*) intensifier is in retrospect doubly-marked — Lavan is over-affirming the kinship-bond at exactly the moment he is preparing to betray it. Alter (1981 p. 56; 2004 p. 152) and Sarna (*JPS* p. 203) both flag the structure.

The WoH preserves the literal *my bone and my flesh* (ASV) against the NRSV/NJPS smoothing to *my own flesh and blood* — the smoothing dissolves the *etzem-va-basar* idiom and its cross-corpus-recurrence.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָבָן֙ לְיַעֲקֹ֔ב הֲכִי־אָחִ֣י אַ֔תָּה וַעֲבַדְתַּ֖נִי חִנָּ֑ם הַגִּ֥ידָה לִּ֖י מַה־מַּשְׂכֻּרְתֶּֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said to Ya'aqov, Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?

paragraphs.text: וּלְלָבָ֖ן שְׁתֵּ֣י בָנ֑וֹת שֵׁ֤ם הַגְּדֹלָה֙ לֵאָ֔ה וְשֵׁ֥ם הַקְּטַנָּ֖ה רָחֵֽל׃

i18n.en: And Lavan had two daughters: the name of the elder was Le'ah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.

paragraphs.text: וְעֵינֵ֥י לֵאָ֖ה רַכּ֑וֹת וְרָחֵל֙ הָֽיְתָ֔ה יְפַת־תֹּ֖אַר וִיפַ֥ת מַרְאֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And Le'ah's eyes were tender; but Rachel was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.

paragraphs.commentary:
***Einei Le'ah rakkot* — *Le'ah's eyes were tender* — is one of the Hebrew Bible's most editorially-consequential lexical disputes.** The adjective *rakh* (feminine plural *rakkot*) has a semantic range spanning *tender / soft / delicate* on one end and *weak / dim / feeble* on the other; the choice between readings determines whether the verse describes Le'ah's beauty-defect or her beauty-feature. Four readings circulate (see [einayim-rakot-leah-eyes-dispute](#einayim-rakot-leah-eyes-dispute)):

- **(a) *Weak* — LXX ἀσθενεῖς; Rashi (a defect from weeping); NRSV / NJPS / NIV.** On this reading Le'ah has a visible eye-flaw and Rachel's whole-body-beauty has a sharp justification.
- **(b) *Tender* — ASV; Alter.** The English *tender* preserves the Hebrew's ambiguity without resolving it.
- **(c) *Lovely* — Onkelos *ya'eyan*; Speiser AB; Gen Rabbah 70:16.** On this reading Le'ah has beautiful eyes as her one feature; the contrast with Rachel is softer.
- **(d) *Soft / delicate* (neutral) — Westermann.** Descriptive antithesis to Rachel's *yefat to'ar*; neither defect nor virtue.

**The WoH defaults to *tender* (ASV/Alter)** — preserving the Hebrew's semantic range rather than disambiguating in either direction. The cost is that *tender* in modern English no longer carries the original ambiguity; the gain is that the dispute is left visible to the reader, with the commentary surfacing the four positions.

***Yefat to'ar v-yefat mar'eh* — *beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance* — deploys the HB's stock beauty-formula** in its **doubled-construct** form. The doubled-form recurs at Gen 39:6 (Yosef) and Esther 2:7 (Esther); the simple-form (*yefat mar'eh* alone) is the formula's standard mode (see [eshet-yefat-mareh](#eshet-yefat-mareh) for the full distribution). The doubled-form marks Rachel's beauty as the chapter's narrative-engine: the fourteen years of labor, the bait-and-switch, and the Le'ah-Rachel rivalry all flow from this verse's establishment of Rachel as the most-beautiful-woman of the patriarchal-corpus.

paragraphs.text: וַיֶּאֱהַ֥ב יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת־רָחֵ֑ל וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֶֽעֱבָדְךָ֙ שֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֔ים בְּרָחֵ֥ל בִּתְּךָ֖ הַקְּטַנָּֽה׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov loved Rachel; and he said, I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֗ן ט֚וֹב תִּתִּ֣י אֹתָ֣הּ לָ֔ךְ מִתִּתִּ֥י אֹתָ֖הּ לְאִ֣ישׁ אַחֵ֑ר שְׁבָ֖ה עִמָּדִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said, It is better that I give her to you, than that I should give her to another man; abide with me.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעֲבֹ֧ד יַעֲקֹ֛ב בְּרָחֵ֖ל שֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֑ים וַיִּהְי֤וּ בְעֵינָיו֙ כְּיָמִ֣ים אֲחָדִ֔ים בְּאַהֲבָת֖וֹ אֹתָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov served seven years for Rachel; and they were in his eyes but a few days, for the love he had to her.

paragraphs.commentary:
***Va-yihyu v-einav k-yamim achadim b-ahavato otah* — *and they were in his eyes as a few days, in his love for her* — is the Hebrew Bible's most-condensed love-formula and a hapax in Genesis.** The verse compresses seven years of labor into *a few days* through the lens of love, framed by the narrator's perception-idiom *b-einav* (in his eyes) and the *b-ahavato* causal-clause (in his love for her).

**The *achadim* lexeme links to Gen 11:1.** The Hebrew *achadim* (plural of *echad*, *one*) used adjectivally for *a few* is rare and editorially-marked. The construction recurs in Genesis only at **Gen 11:1** (*safah achat u-devarim achadim*, *one language and one / a few speech-things* — the Babel pericope's opening) and here at Gen 29:20 (*k-yamim achadim*). The shared lexeme is one of the patriarchal-narrative's quieter inter-textual signals — the Babel-state-of-unified-speech is verbally rhymed with the Ya'aqov-state-of-love-compressed-time. Alter (*Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 153), Westermann (*Genesis 12-36* 1985 p. 468), and Fokkelman (*Narrative Art in Genesis* 1975 p. 127) all flag the verbal-echo; the thematic-conclusion is left open (see [yamim-achadim-jacob-love-for-rachel](#yamim-achadim-jacob-love-for-rachel)).

**The narrator-intervention is editorially-unusual.** The patriarchal-narratives are typically exterior-action narratives; the *b-einav k-yamim achadim* aside is one of the HB's rare-windows into Ya'aqov's interior-life. The comparison is **subjective** — in Ya'aqov's eyes, not objectively. The WoH preserves the *b-einav* idiom (*in his eyes*) and the *b-ahavato* causal-clause (*for the love he had to her*) literally.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֤ב אֶל־לָבָן֙ הָבָ֣ה אֶת־אִשְׁתִּ֔י כִּ֥י מָלְא֖וּ יָמָ֑י וְאָב֖וֹאָה אֵלֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to Lavan, Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.

paragraphs.text: וַיֶּאֱסֹ֥ף לָבָ֛ן אֶת־כָּל־אַנְשֵׁ֥י הַמָּק֖וֹם וַיַּ֥עַשׂ מִשְׁתֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: And Lavan gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י בָעֶ֔רֶב וַיִּקַּח֙ אֶת־לֵאָ֣ה בִתּ֔וֹ וַיָּבֵ֥א אֹתָ֖הּ אֵלָ֑יו וַיָּבֹ֖א אֵלֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Le'ah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in to her.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתֵּ֤ן לָבָן֙ לָ֔הּ אֶת־זִלְפָּ֖ה שִׁפְחָת֑וֹ לְלֵאָ֥ה בִתּ֖וֹ שִׁפְחָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Lavan gave Zilpah his maidservant to his daughter Le'ah for a maidservant.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י בַבֹּ֔קֶר וְהִנֵּה־הִ֖וא לֵאָ֑ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־לָבָ֗ן מַה־זֹּאת֙ עָשִׂ֣יתָ לִּ֔י הֲלֹ֤א בְרָחֵל֙ עָבַ֣דְתִּי עִמָּ֔ךְ וְלָ֖מָּה רִמִּיתָֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass in the morning that, behold, it was Le'ah; and he said to Lavan, What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?

paragraphs.commentary:
**The morning-discovery is among the Hebrew Bible's tersest reveal-moments.** *Va-yhi va-boqer v-hineh hi Le'ah* — *and it came to pass in the morning, and behold, it was Le'ah*. The Hebrew gives no description of the discovery-process, no narration of Ya'aqov's interior-state, no commentary on how the substitution could have escaped notice through the wedding-night; only the bare result and the protest. The narrative-economy is editorially-deliberate: the focus is on the **reversal** that v 26 will articulate, not on the mechanics of the substitution.

*Va-lamah rimitani* — *why have you deceived me?* — uses the verb *ramah* (deceive, beguile). The verb is editorially-marked: Ya'aqov, the man who **deceived** his father Yitzchaq (Gen 27:35, where Yitzchaq says *ba achikha b-mirmah* — *your brother came in deceit* — using the cognate noun *mirmah*), now accuses Lavan of the same offense. The lexical-rhyme between Gen 27's *mirmah* and Gen 29:25's *rimitani* is editorially-deliberate: Ya'aqov is using the precise-vocabulary of the offense he committed against Esav to accuse Lavan of doing the same to him. Alter (1981 p. 45; 2004 p. 153) flags the lexical-rhyme; Sarna (*JPS* p. 205) and Fokkelman (1975 p. 128) concur.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן לֹא־יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בִּמְקוֹמֵ֑נוּ לָתֵ֥ת הַצְּעִירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַבְּכִירָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said, It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.

paragraphs.commentary:
**This is the chapter's editorial-pivot and the foundational ironic-moment of the Jacob-cycle.** Lavan's defense of the bait-and-switch uses the exact lexical-pair — *ha-bekhirah / ha-tze'irah* (the firstborn-daughter / the younger-daughter) — that Ya'aqov himself violated when he supplanted Esav as the *bekhor* (firstborn) at Gen 27. The man who stole the firstborn-blessing in his land of origin now receives the firstborn-daughter in place of the younger he sought. The lexical-rhyme is unmistakable in the Hebrew (see [firstborn-priority-reversal-irony](#firstborn-priority-reversal-irony)):

- **Gen 25:23** — the YHWH-oracle: *u-rav ya'avod tza'ir* (the elder shall serve the **younger**).
- **Gen 25:31-34** — Esav's birthright-sale: the *bekhorah* is the focal noun.
- **Gen 27:19** — Ya'aqov's deception: *anokhi Esav bekhorekha* (I am Esav your **firstborn**).
- **Gen 27:36** — Esav's lament: *ya'qveni zeh pa'amayim et bekhorati laqach* (he took away my **birthright**).
- **Gen 29:26** — Lavan's defense: *latet ha-tze'irah lifnei ha-bekhirah* (to give the **younger** before the **firstborn**).

The *bekhor* / *tza'ir* binary is the same; only the gender is changed. Lavan is delivering — perhaps without knowing it — the chapter's narrative-justice closure: the deceiver is deceived in the lexical-coin of his own deception. Sarna (*JPS* p. 205): *The very terms Laban employs — bekhirah and tze'irah — must have stabbed Jacob with their irony.* Alter (1981 pp. 45-46; 2004 p. 154): *The deceiver is deceived in the lexical-coin of his own deception.* Fokkelman (*Narrative Art in Genesis* 1975 pp. 128-129) treats the inversion exhaustively.

**The pattern continues across the Jacob-line.** Ya'aqov himself, now patriarch, will **cross his hands** at Gen 48:13-20 to bless Ephraim (the younger) over Manasseh (the elder) — knowing exactly what he is doing (*lo avi ki-zeh ha-bekhor*, *no, my father, this one is the firstborn* — Joseph's protest at v 18). The principle established at Gen 25:23, ironically-reversed at Gen 29:26, and ultimately-internalized at Gen 48 becomes a structural-axiom of the Hebrew Bible's election-theology: the chosen line is repeatedly the **non-default heir** (Yosef, Mosheh, David, Solomon — Greenspahn *When Brothers Dwell Together* 1994 treats the full pattern).

The WoH preserves the lexical-pair *ha-tze'irah / ha-bekhirah* (the *younger* / the *firstborn*) literally, matching ASV. The NJPS smoothing to *older* (rather than *firstborn*) is rejected because it dissolves the *bekhir-* / *bekhor-* root-link to Gen 27's *bekhorah* — the very link that makes the irony work.

paragraphs.text: מַלֵּ֖א שְׁבֻ֣עַ זֹ֑את וְנִתְּנָ֨ה לְךָ֜ גַּם־אֶת־זֹ֗את בַּעֲבֹדָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תַּעֲבֹ֣ד עִמָּדִ֔י ע֖וֹד שֶֽׁבַע־שָׁנִ֥ים אֲחֵרֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: Fulfill the week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service which you shall serve with me yet seven other years.

paragraphs.commentary:
***Male shvua zot* — *fulfill the week of this one* — uses *shavua* in the technical sense of *bridal-week*, the seven-day wedding-feast institution of the ancient Near East.** The seven-day-feast is cross-corpus attested at **Judg 14:12, 17** (Shimshon's wedding-feast: *shivat ymei ha-mishteh*, the seven days of the feast — with the riddle-narrative spanning the seven days and the bride-prying-the-answer *ba-yom ha-shvi'i*, on the seventh day). The institution is documented in Old-Babylonian marriage-contracts (Greengus *JCS* 20, 1969); de Vaux *Ancient Israel* 1961 ET 1965 pp. 32-38 places the HB-evidence in its ANE context (see [shavua-bride-week](#shavua-bride-week)).

**The two service-periods are distinct from the bridal-week.** The chapter's seven-day-feast (here at v 27 and at v 28) should not be confused with the two seven-year-service-periods (vv 18, 27, 30). The structural-cluster of **sevens** in the chapter — seven-years × 2, seven-day-feast × 1 — is editorially-marked but the lexical institutions are distinct. The WoH preserves *shavua* literally as *the week* (ASV), trusting the context to convey the bridal-week sense.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֤עַשׂ יַעֲקֹב֙ כֵּ֔ן וַיְמַלֵּ֖א שְׁבֻ֣עַ זֹ֑את וַיִּתֶּן־ל֛וֹ אֶת־רָחֵ֥ל בִּתּ֖וֹ ל֥וֹ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov did so, and fulfilled her week; and he gave him Rachel his daughter to be his wife.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתֵּ֤ן לָבָן֙ לְרָחֵ֣ל בִּתּ֔וֹ אֶת־בִּלְהָ֖ה שִׁפְחָת֑וֹ לָ֖הּ לְשִׁפְחָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Lavan gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah his maidservant to be her maidservant.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹא֙ גַּ֣ם אֶל־רָחֵ֔ל וַיֶּאֱהַ֥ב גַּֽם־אֶת־רָחֵ֖ל מִלֵּאָ֑ה וַיַּעֲבֹ֣ד עִמּ֔וֹ ע֖וֹד שֶֽׁבַע־שָׁנִ֥ים אֲחֵרֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: And he went in also to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Le'ah, and served with him yet seven other years.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֤רְא יְהוָה֙ כִּֽי־שְׂנוּאָ֣ה לֵאָ֔ה וַיִּפְתַּ֖ח אֶת־רַחְמָ֑הּ וְרָחֵ֖ל עֲקָרָֽה׃

i18n.en: And YHWH saw that Le'ah was hated, and he opened her womb; but Rachel was barren.

paragraphs.commentary:
***Va-yiftach et-rachmah* — *and he opened her womb* — deploys the Hebrew Bible's standard divine-fertility-formula.** The construction recurs at **Gen 30:22** (Rachel's later opening: *va-yizkor Elohim et-Rachel ... va-yiftach et-rachmah*) and at **1 Sam 1:19-20** (Channah's conception, with the implicit-opening through *va-yizkereha YHWH*). The formula is the positive-counterpart of the *atzar-rechem* / *sagar-rechem* (close-the-womb) formula already tracked at the existing entry for the Gen 20:18 Avimelekh-Sarah episode. Together the two form the **divine-control-of-the-womb pattern** — fertility presented as conditioned by divine-action, the theological structure that frames the patriarchal-and-prophetic-births across the HB (Yitzchaq from barren-Sarah; Ya'aqov-and-Esav from barren-Rivkah, Gen 25:21; Yosef from initially-barren-Rachel; Shimshon from barren-Manoach's-wife, Judg 13:2-3; Shmuel from initially-barren-Channah). See [patach-rechem-divine-fertility-formula](#patach-rechem-divine-fertility-formula).

***S'nu'ah Le'ah* — *Le'ah was hated*.** The Hebrew *s'nu'ah* (qal passive participle of *sane'*, to hate) has been read two ways: (i) **literal *hated*** (ASV / KJV / Alter / Sarna *JPS*) — the verb in qal carries strong-emotional-rejection force; (ii) **comparative *unloved*** (NRSV / NJPS, on the basis of **Deut 21:15**'s legal-construction *ha-achat ahuvah v-ha-achat s'nu'ah*, *the one beloved and the one unloved*, where *s'nu'ah* is the comparative-opposite of *ahuvah* — *less-loved*, not actively-hated). The text at v 30 (*va-ye'ehav gam et-Rachel mi-Le'ah*, *and he loved Rachel more than Le'ah*) supports the comparative-reading: Ya'aqov does love Le'ah; he loves Rachel more. **The WoH defaults to *hated* (ASV-literal)**, preserving the lexeme's force; the comparative-reading is flagged here. The Le'ah-portrait gains an edge either way: she is the disprized-wife to whom YHWH gives fertility as compensation for the husband's preference.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּ֤הַר לֵאָה֙ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ רְאוּבֵ֑ן כִּ֣י אָֽמְרָ֗ה כִּֽי־רָאָ֤ה יְהוָה֙ בְּעָנְיִ֔י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה יֶאֱהָבַ֥נִי אִישִֽׁי׃

i18n.en: And Le'ah conceived, and bore a son, and she called his name Re'uven; for she said, Because YHWH has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The opening of the four-name-aetiology cluster (vv 32-35) — Le'ah's first four sons: Re'uven, Shim'on, Levi, Yehudah — the foundational naming-pattern for the twelve-tribes naming-tradition.** The four together form a deliberate compositional unit with a verb-progression *ra'ah → shama → lavah → yadah* (see → heard → join → praise) and a subject-progression YHWH → husband → Le'ah-self (see [four-leah-firstborn-name-etymologies-cluster](#four-leah-firstborn-name-etymologies-cluster)).

**Re'uven (רְאוּבֵן).** The folk-etymology is double-anchored: (a) *ra'ah* (see) + *ben* (son) = *re'u-ben*, *see, a son* — the most-immediate wordplay on the name's two syllables; (b) *ki ra'ah YHWH b-onyi* — *because YHWH has seen my affliction* — the verbal-anchor through *ra'ah*. The doubling is editorially-deliberate (Sarna *JPS* p. 207). The name **does not contain the theophoric** *-yah* / *-el* suffix of later Israelite-naming; it preserves the early-period naming-pattern of simple-statements (*Pinchas*, *Eli*, *Shmuel*).

**The downstream tribal-significance.** Re'uven is the firstborn-of-the-firstborn-line; his birth-narrative ends with the love-formula (*atah ye'ehavani ishi*, *now my husband will love me*) that frames Le'ah's entire reproductive-arc across the four sons. The Re'uven-tribe will later lose the firstborn-priority (Gen 49:3-4, Ya'aqov's deathbed-curse for the Bilhah-incident at Gen 35:22); the chapter's first-name is thus also the first-stripped-name in the downstream tribal-narrative — a quiet foreshadowing.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּ֣הַר עוֹד֮ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּן֒ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר כִּֽי־שָׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ כִּֽי־שְׂנוּאָ֣ה אָנֹ֔כִי וַיִּתֶּן־לִ֖י גַּם־אֶת־זֶ֑ה וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ שִׁמְעֽוֹן׃

i18n.en: And she conceived again, and bore a son; and said, Because YHWH has heard that I am hated, he has given me this one also; and she called his name Shim'on.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Shim'on (שִׁמְעוֹן).** The folk-etymology is anchored on *shama* (hear) + *-on* nominalizing-suffix: *Shim'on* = *the heard-one*. The verb-pattern shifts from v 32's *ra'ah* (see) to v 33's *shama* (hear) — the YHWH-perception-verb-pair (see-and-hear) that recurs across the HB (Exod 3:7, *r'oh ra'iti et-oni ami ... v-et-tza'aqatam shamati*; Exod 4:31; the divine-perception standard). The cluster's verbs are editorially-deliberate: divine-perception is given through both visual and auditory channels.

The name-etymology also re-deploys the *s'nu'ah* lexeme from v 31 (*ki s'nu'ah anokhi*, *because I am hated*). Le'ah's self-description as *s'nu'ah* anchors the four-name cluster in her marriage-condition: the four sons are named for what is missing from the marriage (love, attention, attachment, praise-deserving), not from what is present. The naming-pattern is **deprivation-grounded**.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּ֣הַר עוֹד֮ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּן֒ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר עַתָּ֤ה הַפַּ֙עַם֙ יִלָּוֶ֤ה אִישִׁי֙ אֵלַ֔י כִּֽי־יָלַ֥דְתִּי ל֖וֹ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה בָנִ֑ים עַל־כֵּ֥ן קָרָֽא־שְׁמ֖וֹ לֵוִֽי׃

i18n.en: And she conceived again, and bore a son; and said, Now this time will my husband be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons; therefore was his name called Levi.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Levi (לֵוִי).** The folk-etymology is anchored on the root *l-v-h* (lavah — *join, attach, accompany*): *yilaveh* (niphal imperfect 3ms of *lavah*) → *Levi*. The verb-pattern shifts from divine-perception (*ra'ah*, *shama*) to **relational-attachment** — the third son's name turns inward, from YHWH's seeing-and-hearing to the husband's potential-joining.

**The downstream tribal-significance is enormous.** Levi becomes the **priestly-tribe** (Num 3:5-13 — the Levi-tribe is set apart for cultic-service; the Levitical-clergy descends from Levi). The name's *attachment* etymology is post-exilically re-interpreted in cultic-attachment terms (the Levites are *attached* to the priestly-service; cf. Num 18:2-4 *yilavu alecha v-yshartukha*, *they shall be joined to you and serve you*, where the cognate verb is used of the Levitical-priestly relation). Hamilton (NICOT 1995 p. 264) flags the double-deployment: the Gen 29:34 etymology is **woman-centered** (a husband joining his wife) while the cultic-deployment is YHWH-centered (Levites joining the priestly-service) — the same root carries both senses, and the woman-centered original is editorially-preserved here rather than retrojectively-cultic-ized.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּ֨הַר ע֜וֹד וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּ֗ן וַתֹּ֙אמֶר֙ הַפַּ֙עַם֙ אוֹדֶ֣ה אֶת־יְהוָ֔ה עַל־כֵּ֛ן קָרְאָ֥ה שְׁמ֖וֹ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַֽתַּעֲמֹ֖ד מִלֶּֽדֶת׃

i18n.en: And she conceived again, and bore a son; and she said, This time will I praise YHWH; therefore she called his name Yehudah; and she ceased bearing.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Yehudah (יְהוּדָה) — the cluster's climactic fourth name.** The folk-etymology is anchored on the verb *yadah* (hiphil: *praise, give thanks*): *odeh* (1cs hiphil imperfect) → *Yehudah*. Critically, the name **contains the tetragrammaton consonants Y-H-W** embedded in *Y-H-W-D-H*; Yehudah is the **only** of Le'ah's first-four sons whose name is **theophoric** through the YHWH-stem.

**The verb-progression closes.** The cluster's four verbs *ra'ah → shama → yilaveh → odeh* (see → heard → join → praise) move from divine-perception, through relational-attachment, to direct-praise. The subject-progression closes the same arc: YHWH-acts (vv 32-33), husband-acts (v 34), Le'ah-acts (v 35). The fourth name is the **first** where Le'ah is the subject of the etymological-verb — the only name in the cluster where her own emotional-state is the foreground rather than the relational-deficit. Fokkelman (*Narrative Art in Genesis* 1975 pp. 130-135) reads this as Le'ah's narrative-arrival: by the fourth son she has shifted from the disprized-wife (v 31) to the praising-mother (v 35).

**The downstream significance is the highest of the four.** Yehudah becomes the **royal-tribe** (Gen 49:8-12 — the Yehudah-blessing; the *shevet mi-Yehudah*, *the sceptre from Yehudah*, establishes the royal-promise that is read messianically across the HB and into the Christian-NT); the **Davidic-dynasty** descends from Yehudah; the **post-exilic community** is named for the tribe (*Yehudim* — Jews). The naming-progression is climactic: it culminates in the name that will name the post-exilic people.

***Va-ta'amod mi-ledet* — *and she ceased bearing*.** The closing-formula marks the narrative-pause before the Bilhah-Zilpah cycle resumes at Gen 30. The four-name-cluster is editorially-closed; the next pericope will deploy the same naming-pattern through the surrogate-births.
